items.prompt: Priya is the only person who understands the payments-retry queue. What does that make the retry queue's bus factor?
choices: 6 — the size of the on-call rotation that's technically assigned to cover payments
1 — only one person's absence is enough to stop the team from maintaining it
0 — bus factor is a concept that only applies to whole teams, never to individual systems
Undefined until someone actually leaves the company and the gap becomes visible
items.explanation: Bus factor counts how many people could disappear before a system becomes unmaintainable by the remaining team. Only one person (Priya) has to be unreachable for the retry queue to become effectively unmaintainable, so its bus factor is 1 — regardless of how many other people are technically on the pager rotation.
items.reference:
🧑‍💻 Priya → Retry queue

Why: bus factor = how many people could disappear before the team can no longer maintain the system — here, exactly one.

items.prompt: A team of 8 engineers has a billing-reconciliation script that only one of them, Tam, has ever modified. What's the bus factor of that script?
choices: 8, since the whole team could theoretically read the code if they sat down with it
1 — Tam is the only person whose absence would stop the team from confidently changing it
It can't be determined at all without first knowing how complex the script actually is
4, since roughly half the team could probably figure it out eventually with enough time
items.explanation: Bus factor isn't about team size or theoretical ability to read code eventually — it's about how many people currently have working knowledge of the system. Team size (8) is irrelevant here; what matters is that exactly one person (Tam) has that knowledge today.
items.reference:
🧑‍💻 Priya → Retry queue

Why: bus factor = how many people could disappear before the team can no longer maintain the system — here, exactly one.

items.prompt: After the incident, the team pairs Dana with Priya on two real changes to the retry queue, so Dana now also has working context. What happens to the retry queue's bus factor?
choices: It stays at 1 — only the original author who wrote the code from scratch ever counts
It rises to 2 — two people now have working context, so either one's absence alone no longer stops the team
It becomes irrelevant the moment any documentation exists for the retry queue at all
It rises to 8, the full team size, since documentation was written during the pairing
items.explanation: Bus factor moves specifically with how many people have real, working knowledge — not with team size or the existence of some documentation. Dana pairing on real changes is what raises it from 1 to 2, because now either Priya or Dana being unreachable still leaves someone who can act.
items.reference:
🧑‍💻 Priya → Retry queue

Why: bus factor = how many people could disappear before the team can no longer maintain the system — here, exactly one.

items.prompt: The team adds Marcus to the payments on-call pager rotation, but he's never opened the retry-queue code. Does that fix the bus-factor problem?
choices: Yes — anyone added to the pager rotation counts toward bus factor automatically by being on the list
No — being paged and having working context are two separate things; the pager schedule spreads who responds, not what they know
Yes, but only once the rotation has grown to at least 3 people covering the system
No, because bus factor can only ever be fixed by the team hiring more engineers outright
items.explanation: A pager rotation determines who gets notified; it says nothing about whether that person has the knowledge to act. Marcus being on the rotation with zero context on this specific system leaves the bus factor at 1 in every way that matters during an actual incident.
items.reference:
📟 On pager rotation
🧠 Has working context on THIS system

Why: these are two separate things — a rotation schedule only guarantees the first one.

items.prompt: What's the difference between 'who gets paged' and 'who could actually resolve this incident quickly'?
choices: There's no meaningful difference — a rotation schedule already guarantees both outcomes
'Who gets paged' is decided by a schedule; 'who could resolve it quickly' depends on who actually has working knowledge of the specific system that broke
The second group is always a strict subset of the first group, by the rotation's own definition
The difference between the two only really matters for systems older than a year
items.explanation: A schedule assigns responsibility for responding; it doesn't check whether the assigned person has relevant knowledge. Those are genuinely independent — a well-run rotation can still page someone with zero context on the system that's actually broken.
items.reference:
📟 On pager rotation
🧠 Has working context on THIS system

Why: these are two separate things — a rotation schedule only guarantees the first one.

items.prompt: A manager says 'we have on-call covered, there's always someone scheduled.' Per L1, why might that statement still leave the team exposed?
choices: It can't still leave the team exposed — a schedule with zero gaps means the risk is fully handled
Because 'covered' by a schedule doesn't mean the scheduled person has working knowledge of whatever system happens to break that night
Because on-call schedules, per this unit, are only ever useful for purely non-technical issues
It's only a real problem in cases where the rotation has fewer than 4 total people on it
items.explanation: A gap-free schedule guarantees a warm body responds — it says nothing about whether that person can actually diagnose the specific system involved. The exposure is knowledge distribution, not staffing, and a schedule alone doesn't touch it.
items.reference:
📟 On pager rotation
🧠 Has working context on THIS system

Why: these are two separate things — a rotation schedule only guarantees the first one.

Not by itself — single ownership is a real trade-off, not an inherent error; the mistake was doing nothing for 8 months to reduce the bus factor it created

items.reference:
Single-owner

Deep expertise, bus factor 1

Collective

Spread knowledge, more coordination cost

Why: neither model is automatically correct — each carries a real cost.

It guarantees, by itself, that the system in question will never contain bugs

The unit's point is that this benefit has to be weighed against the bus-factor risk, not that the benefit doesn't exist.
items.reference:
Single-owner

Collective

Spread knowledge, more coordination cost

Why: neither model is automatically correct — each carries a real cost.

items.prompt: A teammate argues 'collective ownership is strictly better, so every team should switch to it immediately.' What does L1 suggest is missing from that argument?
choices: Nothing — L1 fully agrees that collective ownership is always the objectively better choice

items.explanation: L1 presents both models as trade-offs, not a hierarchy. Collective ownership lowers bus-factor risk but costs more ongoing effort to keep consistent and high-quality — treating it as a free upgrade skips that real cost.
items.reference:
Single-owner

Deep expertise, bus factor 1

Collective

Spread knowledge, more coordination cost

Why: neither model is automatically correct — each carries a real cost.

items.prompt: Per L1, what is a runbook actually for?
choices: A record kept specifically to assign blame to whoever caused the incident afterward
A written, checked-in procedure that lets whoever is on-call — not just the original author — act with real context during an incident
A performance review document used to evaluate the on-call engineer's response
A replacement for ever having engineers genuinely understand the system at all
items.explanation: A runbook exists specifically to transfer the original author's context onto paper (or into a repo) so someone else can act on it under pressure. It's not about assigning blame or replacing engineering understanding — it's a substitute for memory that isn't in the room.
items.reference:
📓 Runbook → Context, on paper, for whoever is on-call

Why: a runbook substitutes for the original author's memory when that author isn't reachable.

items.prompt: Marcus has no runbook and no prior context on the retry queue. What does that combination force him to do during the incident?
choices: Nothing different from normal — the code is treated as self-explanatory to any engineer who reads it
Read unfamiliar source code cold, under time pressure, and reconstruct the author's reasoning from scratch
Simply wait for the codebase to auto-generate documentation explaining the retry logic
Immediately know the exact fix on sight, purely because he's an experienced engineer
items.explanation: With no runbook and no prior exposure, Marcus's only tool is the raw code itself — he has to reconstruct, live and under pressure, the reasoning Priya already had in her head. That reconstruction is exactly what ate most of the three hours.
items.reference:
📓 Runbook → Context, on paper, for whoever is on-call

Why: a runbook substitutes for the original author's memory when that author isn't reachable.

No — Marcus lacked access to knowledge Priya already had, which is a knowledge-distribution problem, not a skill problem

It's genuinely impossible to know without gathering more background information about Marcus

🧑‍💻 Priya — same skill level, has context

🧑‍💻 Priya — same skill level, has context

choices: Single-owner, because it reliably and consistently produces a deeper, more durable kind of technical expertise
Collective, because spreading ownership across more people always lowers bus factor down to a genuinely safe level
Neither, in the abstract — the right call depends on how costly it is if the single owner is unreachable at the wrong moment, weighed against the coordination cost of shared ownership
Whichever ownership model the majority of the team happens to personally prefer at any given time
items.explanation: L2 explicitly resists naming a universal winner — it frames the choice as depending on the actual cost of unreachability for that specific system, against the real coordination cost collective ownership adds. A batch job run quarterly and a system that pages someone at 2 AM don't need the same answer.
items.reference:
Low incident costSingle-owner can be fine
Pages someone at 2 AMNeeds more than one owner

Why: the right model depends on the cost of the owner being unreachable at the wrong moment.

A quarterly, on-request script has a low cost if the owner is briefly unavailable — very different from a system that pages someone at 2 AM, where the same bus factor of 1 is a real problem.

items.prompt: Why does L2 say a system that pages someone at 2 AM cannot stay single-owned, even if the single owner is excellent?

However good the single owner is, single ownership alone gives no guarantee that someone else can act when they're asleep, traveling, or otherwise unavailable — which is exactly the guarantee on-call needs.

items.prompt: In `chargeWithRetry`, what actual condition triggers a duplicate charge?
choices: The payment provider's own API silently and independently double-charges on its end
A confirmation that arrives after the 30-second timeout still gets processed as a success, but the retry had already fired at the 30-second mark and also succeeded
Two different customers accidentally end up using the exact same credit card number
The retry queue mistakenly runs the same charge twice because of a plain typo in the loop
items.explanation: The bug is a genuine race: `Promise.race` treats a confirmation arriving even slightly after 30 seconds as a timeout and fires a retry, but the original confirmation still lands and succeeds too — both charges go through, none of them individually 'wrong.'
items.reference:
t=0s: charge submitted
t=30s: timeout fires → retry submitted
t=34s: original confirmation ALSO arrives → succeeds
Result: 2 successful charges

Why: the retry timer doesn't check whether the original attempt actually failed or was just slow.

items.prompt: What specific check is missing from `chargeWithRetry` that would have prevented the duplicate charge?

A check for whether the original attempt actually failed, versus simply running long, before submitting a retry
A check that validates the customer's billing address before any retry attempt is made
A hard retry limit — the function should simply refuse to ever retry more than once
items.explanation: The 30-second timeout assumes 'no confirmation yet' means 'the original attempt failed,' but it could just mean 'still in flight.' The missing safeguard is distinguishing a genuinely failed attempt from a slow-but-succeeding one before firing a retry.
items.reference:
t=0s: charge submitted
t=30s: timeout fires → retry submitted
t=34s: original confirmation ALSO arrives → succeeds
Result: 2 successful charges

Why: the retry timer doesn't check whether the original attempt actually failed or was just slow.

items.reference:
